old:
Commercial bank: a bank that accepts deposits from households and firms, makes loans to them, and provides a payments system — profiting from the interest rate spread. Its three functions: accepting deposits (sight and time accounts), lending, and providing a payments mechanism.

Investment bank: takes no public deposits; it underwrites share and bond issues, advises on takeovers and trades securities for large firms, governments and institutions — higher risk, funded from wholesale markets. Many banks do both, which raises systemic risk.

  • Lending.
  • Providing a payments mechanism.

Investment bank: takes no public deposits; it underwrites share and bond issues, advises on takeovers and trades securities for large firms, governments and institutions — higher risk, funded from wholesale markets.

old:
Assets = Liabilities + Capital, always. Deposits are liabilities — the bank owes them back to customers; loans are assets — borrowers owe them to the bank. Getting that backwards is the classic error.

Liabilities: customer deposits (largest), bonds issued and wholesale borrowing. Assets, in descending order of liquidity: cash and central-bank balances, bills, then loans and advances — the least liquid but most profitable, and normally the largest.

old:
Liquidity (meet withdrawals on demand — survival), profitability (maximise returns for shareholders) and security (minimise losses from bad debts).

The central conflict is liquidity vs profitability: the most liquid assets earn the least, the most profitable are the least liquid — too little liquidity risks a bank run, too much sacrifices profit. And profitability vs security: higher returns come only from riskier lending, whose defaults can wipe out the bank's capital.

  • Security (minimise losses from bad debts).

old:
Credit creation: the process by which commercial banks make loans that create new bank deposits, thereby increasing the money supply. A new loan credits the borrower's account with a new deposit — banks do not merely lend out savers' money.

It rests on fractional reserve banking: only a fraction of deposits is ever withdrawn at once, so banks hold a fraction as reserves and lend the rest; each loan becomes someone else's deposit and the cycle repeats, multiplying deposits. Credit growth drives AD — and excessive growth feeds inflation and asset bubbles.

old:
Central bank: a national bank that provides financial and banking services for a country's government and commercial banks — in the UK, the Bank of England.

Its functions: issuing currency, managing the money supply, setting interest rates, acting as lender of last resort in crises, and regulating and supervising banks.
new:
Central bank: a national bank that provides financial and banking services for a country's government and commercial banks — in the UK, the Bank of England.

Its functions:

  • Issuing currency.
  • Managing the money supply.
  • Setting interest rates.
  • Acting as lender of last resort in crises.
  • Regulating and supervising banks.

old:
The MPC's rate changes reach AD through three channels. Consumption: cheaper borrowing, less reward for saving, and variable-rate mortgage holders keep more disposable income. Investment: firms' cost of borrowing falls, so more projects pay.

Net exports: lower returns send hot money abroad, the extra supply of pounds depreciates the currency, exports cheapen and imports dearen. All three raise AD — and a rate rise runs the whole mechanism in reverse.
new:
The MPC's rate changes reach AD through three channels:

  • Consumption: cheaper borrowing, less reward for saving, and variable-rate mortgage holders keep more disposable income.
  • Investment: firms' cost of borrowing falls, so more projects pay.
  • Net exports: lower returns send hot money abroad, the extra supply of pounds depreciates the currency, exports cheapen and imports dearen.

All three raise AD — and a rate rise runs the whole mechanism in reverse.

old:
Time lags — effects can take up to two years; fixed-rate borrowers feel nothing at first. The liquidity trap — near the zero lower bound, further cuts change little, which is why QE exists at all.

Asset price bubbles — cheap money inflates housing and shares, and bursting bubbles bring crises. And confidence — in a recession, households save the windfall and firms delay investment regardless of the rate. Monetary policy pulls on a string it cannot push.

  • Asset price bubbles — cheap money inflates housing and shares, and bursting bubbles bring crises.
  • Confidence — in a recession, households save the windfall and firms delay investment regardless of the rate.

Monetary policy pulls on a string it cannot push.

old:
Liquidity ratio: the proportion of a bank's assets that are held in liquid form, such as cash, reserves at the central bank and easily marketable securities — liquid assets ÷ total assets × 100. It guards against illiquidity: being unable to meet withdrawals, the bank-run failure of borrowing short and lending long.

Capital ratio: capital ÷ risk-weighted assets × 100. Capital absorbs losses when borrowers default; once losses exceed it, the bank is insolvent.
new:

Capital ratio: capital ÷ risk-weighted assets × 100.

old:
Systemic risk: the risk that the failure of one financial institution triggers the failure of others and a wider financial crisis — interbank lending, shared assets and confidence spread failure by contagion (Lehman Brothers, 2008). Moral hazard: too-big-to-fail banks take excessive risks expecting bailouts (RBS and Lloyds).

The trade-off: the tools that contain systemic risk — deposit insurance, lender of last resort, bailouts — are the very tools that create moral hazard; and the capital and liquidity rules that make banks safer also restrict credit creation and growth. Regulators can fully eliminate neither risk.

old:
Fiscal policy is the government's manipulation of government spending (G) and taxation (T) to meet macroeconomic objectives — with microeconomic functions too, such as correcting market failures and changing incentives.

Expansionary: raise G, cut T — AD rises. Contractionary: cut G, raise T — AD falls. Spending on education, infrastructure and R&D also works on the supply side, shifting LRAS.
new:
Fiscal policy is the government's manipulation of government spending (G) and taxation (T) to meet macroeconomic objectives — with microeconomic functions too, such as correcting market failures and changing incentives.

  • Expansionary: raise G, cut T — AD rises.
  • Contractionary: cut G, raise T — AD falls.

Spending on education, infrastructure and R&D also works on the supply side, shifting LRAS.

old:
Current expenditure — day-to-day spending on public-sector wages and consumables (teachers' pay, medicines). Capital expenditure — long-term investment in assets such as infrastructure. Transfer payments — payments with no output in return, such as benefits and pensions (excluded from G in AD).

Taxes exist to fund this spending, manage AD, correct market failures and redistribute income.
new:
• Current expenditure — day-to-day spending on public-sector wages and consumables (teachers' pay, medicines).
  • Capital expenditure — long-term investment in assets such as infrastructure.
  • Transfer payments — payments with no output in return, such as benefits and pensions (excluded from G in AD).

Taxes exist to fund this spending, manage AD, correct market failures and redistribute income.

old:
Progressive — the average tax rate rises with income (UK income tax). Proportional — the same rate at every income. Regressive — the average rate falls as income rises, taking a bigger share from the poor (duties, VAT in practice).

The principles of taxation ask taxes to be equitable, efficient, certain and convenient — the mix of direct taxes (on income and profits) and indirect taxes (on spending) is judged against these.
new:
• Progressive — the average tax rate rises with income (UK income tax).
  • Proportional — the same rate at every income.
  • Regressive — the average rate falls as income rises, taking a bigger share from the poor (duties, VAT in practice).

The principles of taxation ask taxes to be equitable, efficient, certain and convenient — the mix of direct taxes (on income and profits) and indirect taxes (on spending) is judged against these.

old:
Supply-side policies are government measures to raise the economy's productive potential, shifting LRAS right. Supply-side improvements are the capacity gains themselves — and AQA stresses they often originate in the private sector, through productivity gains, innovation and investment, independently of government.

Policy divides into market-based (removing intervention) and interventionist (government spending) approaches.
new:

old:
Free-market: tax cuts to sharpen incentives, privatisation, deregulation, labour-market reforms. Interventionist: government spending on education and training, industrial policy, subsidising research and development.

By improving skills, mobility and incentives, both routes can lower the natural rate of unemployment — the frictional and structural core that demand policy cannot touch — while raising potential output and the trend growth rate.

old:
Trade liberalisation — falling tariffs and quotas (China's WTO entry in 2001 transformed its trade); advances in transport and communication technology; the growth of MNCs building global supply chains (Apple, Amazon, Unilever); and containerisation, which slashed shipping costs and time.

Plus the deregulation of financial markets in the 1990s freeing capital flows, and global institutions — the WTO, IMF and World Bank — promoting free trade and investment.

Workers: jobs and rising wages in developing countries — against job losses where production relocates. Firms: bigger markets, cheaper inputs and economies of scale — against fiercer competition and fragile supply chains.

Governments: growth and tax revenue — against inequality and exposure to external shocks. The environment mostly loses: more production, transport, emissions and resource exploitation.

old:
Germany's PPF runs from 150mn T-shirts to 20mn chips; Vietnam's from 200mn T-shirts to 10mn chips — each has an absolute advantage in one good. Opportunity costs: a chip costs Germany 7.5 T-shirts but Vietnam 20; a T-shirt costs Vietnam 0.05 chips but Germany 0.13.

Each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower: fully specialised, they produce 20m chips and 200mn T-shirts — beating the 15m and 175mn made without specialisation — and by trading, both consume beyond their own PPFs.

The pattern of trade — what is traded and with whom — shifts with comparative advantage (UK manufacturing's decline), emerging economies, trade blocs and agreements (Brexit), and relative exchange rates.

old:
A customs union (e.g. MERCOSUR) removes tariffs and quotas between members and adds a common external tariff; a free trade area lacks the common tariff, a common market (the EU) adds free movement of labour and capital.

Trade creation: trade shifts to a lower-cost producer inside the bloc — welfare rises. Trade diversion: it shifts from a cheaper outsider to a dearer member — welfare falls. The WTO promotes trade liberalisation as negotiating forum and dispute court — in tension with blocs that favour their members.

old:
Balance of payments (BoP): records all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Inflows are credits, outflows debits.

The current account: trade in goods and services, primary income (profits, interest, dividends) and secondary income (aid, remittances). The capital account: minor capital transfers such as debt forgiveness. The financial account: FDI, portfolio investment and reserve changes — and since the BoP must balance, a current account deficit is financed by a capital and financial account surplus.
new:
Balance of payments (BoP): records all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Inflows are credits, outflows debits.

  • The current account: trade in goods and services, primary income (profits, interest, dividends) and secondary income (aid, remittances).
  • The capital account: minor capital transfers such as debt forgiveness.
  • The financial account: FDI, portfolio investment and reserve changes.

Since the BoP must balance, a current account deficit is financed by a capital and financial account surplus.

old:
Causes: low competitiveness (weak productivity or high inflation against rivals), a strong exchange rate, high domestic demand sucking in imports, and structural decline such as a shrinking manufacturing base.

Persistent deficits build foreign debt and can trigger currency depreciation and weaker FDI as confidence erodes; persistent surpluses feed inflation and over-reliance on exports, leaving the economy exposed to global downturns.

  • High domestic demand sucking in imports.
  • Structural decline such as a shrinking manufacturing base.

Persistent deficits build foreign debt and can trigger currency depreciation and weaker FDI as confidence erodes.

Persistent surpluses feed inflation and over-reliance on exports, leaving the economy exposed to global downturns.

old:
Expenditure-switching (tariffs, quotas, devaluation) redirects demand towards domestic output — quick, but invites retaliation and raises consumer prices. Expenditure-reducing (contractionary fiscal policy, higher interest rates) cuts demand and imports together — at the price of slower growth and higher unemployment.

Supply-side policies (education, R&D, infrastructure) rebuild export competitiveness — the durable fix, but slow and costly. Each route trades the current account against other macro objectives.
new:
• Expenditure-switching (tariffs, quotas, devaluation) redirects demand towards domestic output — quick, but invites retaliation and raises consumer prices.
  • Expenditure-reducing (contractionary fiscal policy, higher interest rates) cuts demand and imports together — at the price of slower growth and higher unemployment.
  • Supply-side policies (education, R&D, infrastructure) rebuild export competitiveness — the durable fix, but slow and costly.

Each route trades the current account against other macro objectives.

old:
Higher demand for the currency shifts D1 right to D2 along the supply curve: the exchange rate rises from P1 to P2. Demand rises with higher relative interest rates (hot money), lower relative inflation, a current account surplus, FDI inflows and bullish speculation.

Supply moves it the other way: QE and speculative selling expand the currency's supply and depreciate it.
new:

Demand rises with:

  • Higher relative interest rates (hot money).
  • Lower relative inflation.
  • A current account surplus.
  • FDI inflows.
  • Bullish speculation.

Supply moves it the other way: QE and speculative selling expand the currency's supply and depreciate it.

old:
After a depreciation the current account worsens first: contracts fix prices in the short run and consumers are slow to switch, so PEDx and PEDm are inelastic. Only as they adjust does the balance improve through the long run — tracing a J.

The Marshall-Lerner condition: a depreciation improves the current account only if PEDx + PEDm > 1. If combined demand is inelastic, it worsens instead.

old:
A currency union (the Eurozone) adds a single currency to a common market. Success needs synchronised business cycles, labour mobility, fiscal transfers to cushion shocked regions, and mobility of capital.

For members: lower transaction costs, price transparency, more trade and investment, no exchange-rate risk. Against: the loss of independent monetary policy and exchange-rate flexibility — leaving members exposed when asymmetric shocks hit.

old:
Economic growth: the narrower concept, measured by rises in real GDP. Economic development: a broader concept. It includes economic growth but also considers improvements in living standards, welfare, and quality of life.

Measures: single indicators (infant mortality, literacy) give partial pictures; composite indicators combine them — the UN's HDI weights health (life expectancy), education (schooling years) and income (real GNI per capita at PPP) equally, scoring 0 to 1.

  • Composite indicators combine them — the UN's HDI weights health (life expectancy), education (schooling years) and income (real GNI per capita at PPP) equally, scoring 0 to 1.

old:
Economic: primary product dependency (volatile prices, Dutch disease); the savings gap — the Harrod-Domar model ties growth to savings and investment; the foreign currency gap; capital flight; demographics; debt servicing; poor access to credit; weak infrastructure; inadequate education and skills; and the absence of property rights, which kills the incentive to invest.

Non-economic: corruption, poor governance and instability, conflict, and geography.

Economic

old:
Market-orientated: trade liberalisation, FDI promotion, subsidy removal, floating exchange rates, microfinance, privatisation — free market forces drive development. Interventionist: human capital investment, protectionism, managed exchange rates, infrastructure, joint ventures, buffer stocks — the state corrects market failure.

Aid comes as humanitarian aid (emergency relief), debt relief (freeing resources for investment) and Official Development Assistance — soft loans and grants, effective unless dependency or corruption blunts them.

  • Infrastructure.
  • Joint ventures.
  • Buffer stocks.
